newsitem.title: USA: Columbia crew may have to pick up satellite early.
newsitem.headline: Columbia crew may have to pick up satellite early.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Columbia may have to pick up a prototype space factory early because it is drifting too close to a space telescope, NASA officials said on Sunday.

The Wake Shield Facility, which was set free from Columbia on Friday night, was not due to be recovered until early Tuesday morning, but the shuttle may have to fly in and get it early on Monday, mission control told the astronauts.

The saucer-shaped prototype space factory has drifted to within 24 miles (39 km) of the Orfeus-Spas telescope, released by the astronauts last Tuesday. The two spacecraft must be at least 12.5 miles apart when the shuttle collects the Wake Shield, NASA spokesman Doug Ward said.
The space factory was designed to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. They could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones.
"We may have to call on you guys to roll with it a bit today," spacecraft communicator Bill McArthur said after waking the astronauts at about 2 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Sunday.

"Overnight we've noticed Spas getting just a little bit close to Wake Shield, and I wanted to give you a heads-up that we are looking at the criteria that might require you to go in and do a retreival at the end of today," McArthur said.
The problem arose when the telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin upper atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up, causing it to approach the Wake Shield.

For five hours overnight, astronomers scaled back their observations with the telescope so it could be placed in a more aerodynamic position to reduce the rate at which it is closing in on the Wake Shield.
This is the first time NASA has flown the shuttle in formation with two recoverable satellites. Flight director Al Pennington said before the mission that doing so would be "tricky."
The five astronauts, who are one-third of the way through a 16-day mission, took six hours off duty on Sunday. They were expected to make private calls to their families.

If the astronauts are instructed to collect the Wake Shield, it will be plucked from orbit with the Shuttle's robot arm at about 2:45 a.m. EST (0745 GMT) on Monday. The decision whether to collect it will be made around 11 p.m. EST on Sunday (0400 GMT on Monday), flight director Rob Kelso said.
Shuttle commander Ken Cockrell said his crew was prepared to work late to collect the satellite if necessary.
"The crew is ready and willing to stay up almost as late as you'd like to make that happen as late as possible, so that Wake Shield can get some more of its work completed," he told mission control.

Four of the factory's seven planned semiconductor manufacturing runs had been completed by Sunday afternoon, and two more can be finished even if the satellite has to be collected early, NASA commentator Eileen Hawley said.
